newsitem.title: GERMANY: German cattle remain free of mad cow disease - Bonn.
newsitem.headline: German cattle remain free of mad cow disease - Bonn.

text.p: Bonn's Agriculture Ministry said on Monday it was confident that Germany remained free of home-grown mad cow disease, despite irregularities in the registration of a cow which died of the sickness.

The calf in question died of bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE) last December, sparking fears that it could be the first German-born cow to fall victim to the disease, which is believed to be a threat to humans.

Until December there had been over 165,000 cases of BSE in Britain, but just four in Germany, all in cows imported from Britain. Germany, one of the toughest advocates of sanctions against Britain, insists its own stocks are free of BSE.
"You can't rule out anything 100 percent, but all the indications are that German cows do not present any BSE risk," Agriculture Ministry State Secretary Franz-Josef Fieter told a news conference.
German authorities base their assertion on the fact that there is no evidence of any German livestock farmer using contaminated protein feed -- the standard route of infection.
The only other infection route which scientists consider potentially viable is from mother to calf -- meaning that any infection must in theory originate from British stock.
However, confusion still surrounds the origin of the calf which died in the village of Hoexter last December.

An agriculture official from Mecklenburg-Vorpommern state conceded on Monday that the cow's identity had not been properly verified when it was first registered, and that its parentage was therefore not clear.
Genetic tests on the cow's presumed relatives may take four weeks or more to establish the identity of its mother.
If the cow's mother is found to have died of BSE, and the calf was born in Germany, this would provide evidence for the theory that a mother can infect a calf with BSE.
In this case, authorities are likely to order the slaughter of 14,000 cows directly descended from British and Swiss imports.
They have already ordered the slaughter of more than 5,000 cows imported from Britain and Switzerland -- the other country where BSE is widespread.
